Content Based Image Retrival (CBIR)

To find the most similar images, CBIR compares the content of the input image to the database images. For this reason, CBIR is also known as query by image content (QBIC)

We represent an image as a vector. There are two ways to extract those features:

  1. Global Approach: try to find a single descriptor to represent the whole image
    • Characterise color spaces, such as color moments (mean, variance, …), color histograms, texture, shape, spatial information
      • They do not work well, a lot of images have the same color histogram but with different contents (e.g. red car and a red building)
    • Not invariant under scaling and rotation, also invariant for intensity, like day-night photos of the Pisa tower
  1. Local Approach: describe visual patterns or structures identifiable in small groups of pixels (edges, points, and various image patches)

For local approaches we need to:

  1. Keypoints detection
  1. Keypoints description → features
  1. Features matching for the different keypoints

Scale Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT)

Edges are not rotation invariant and not even scaling invariant

A corner is the intersection of two edges

  • point whose local neighbourhood exhibits significant intensity (or gradient) changes in multiple directions
  • they are rotation invariant but not scale invariant

A Blob is a circular flat region (thus rotational invariant and scale invariant) in an image

  • thus can be used as a local feature because both scale and rotation invariant

In one dimension there are two abrubt intensity changes → composition of two step signal

  • In small blobs the two peaks start overlapping, until they become one
    • The convolved signal exhibits a global minimum exactly at the center of the blob
    • local minima / local maxima because in the image could be a lot of blobs

It’s equivalent of changing the σ\sigmaσ﻿ of the LOG operator (more or less)

  • Laplacian response decays as scale (σ\sigmaσ﻿) increases thus we must scale it by σ2\sigma^2σ2﻿ to get a scale-invariant operator
    • scale normalized BLOB → NBLOB
    • decreases because the steepness of the border tends to decrease

Post Processing

There is a phase of post-processing of the features vectors

  1. ψi←max⁡(ψi,0.2∣∣ψ∣∣)\psi_i \larr \max (\psi_i, 0.2 ||\psi||)ψi​←max(ψi​,0.2∣∣ψ∣∣)﻿ to reduce the impact of non-linear intensity changes
    • low pass filter between components
  1. Normalize, so that ∣∣ψ∣∣=512||\psi|| = 512∣∣ψ∣∣=512﻿
  1. Quantize to 8 bit, thus ψi←min⁡(⌊ψi⌋,28−1)\psi_i \larr \min(\lfloor \psi_i \rfloor, 2^8-1)ψi​←min(⌊ψi​⌋,28−1)﻿
    • Divide by 4 the dimension wrt a 32 bit int

The resulting vector is the SIFT feature descriptor corresponding to the detected key-point.

  • Thus I will have a set of SIFT feature descriptors per image

Feature Matching

Nearest Neighbour Search

  • Given two images AAA﻿A,BA, BA,B﻿BBB﻿A,BA, BA,B﻿NaN_aNa​﻿NA,NBN_A, N_BNA​,NB​﻿and NbN_bNb​﻿
    • Given ψa\psi_aψa​﻿ find ψb=arg min⁡ψi∈Nb∣∣ψi−ψa∣∣\psi_b = \argmin _{\psi_i \in N_b} ||\psi_i - \psi_a||ψb​=argminψi​∈Nb​​∣∣ψi​−ψa​∣∣﻿
  • Then I will sum for all images and the ones above a certain thresholds will pass

A pair of descriptors is considered reliable only if its absolute distance is below a certain threshold

  • Descriptor pairs with a distance above the threshold are outliers.
  • However, the setting of the threshold is problematic, since some descriptors can be at very short distances, while some other descriptors can lie far away

Instead of using an absolute distance threshold, a more reliable approach relies on
the first-to-second nearest neighbor distance ratio (NNDR).

  • For a descriptor ψa∈NAψ_a ∈ N_Aψa​∈NA​﻿, we compute the two closest descriptors ψ1b∈NBψ_1 ^b ∈ N_Bψ1b​∈NB​﻿ and ψ2b∈NBψ_2^b ∈ N_Bψ2b​∈NB​﻿ according to L2L_2L2​﻿ we get:
  • If NNDR→0\text{NNDR} \rarr 0NNDR→0﻿ the second-NN is very distant, and the descriptor is considered reliable
    • empirically a reletive threshold of 0.80.80.8﻿ guaratees a good separation

Is it robust this procedure? If I add a small random noise to all descriptors, the result will be the same?

  • It could be significant just for roundings, smoothing and approximation during the phases before

Computing the NNNNNN﻿ with all the collection is complex O(∣NA∣×nTOT×d)O(|N_A|\times n_{\text{TOT}} \times d)O(∣NA​∣×nTOT​×d)﻿

  • For feature points with a limited numbers of dimensions (up to 10) there are data structures, such as KD trees, that can improve the search performance over the brute force approach, but they are not suitable for SIFT descriptors

Approximate NN search (ANN)

Given Ψ={ψ1,...,ψn}\Psi = \{ \psi_1, ..., \psi_n \}Ψ={ψ1​,...,ψn​}﻿ the image collection feature descriptors

We have also a codebook C={μ1,...,μk}C = \{ \mu_1, ..., \mu_k\}C={μ1​,...,μk​}﻿ with μi∈Rk\mu_i \in R^{k}μi​∈Rk﻿

A vector quantizer q:Ψ→Cq: \Psi \rarr Cq:Ψ→C﻿ maps a vector ψi\psi_iψi​﻿ to it’s closest codeword q(ψi)q(\psi_i)q(ψi​)﻿

We have a Voronoi cell ViV_iVi​﻿ associated to every codeword μi∈C\mu_i \in Cμi​∈C﻿ (Voronoi tessellation)

Now that I have quantize each feature vector, I can save it as an index iii﻿

  • The codebook C∗C^*C∗﻿ (optimal) is found by minimizing the approximation error
  • Then the distance is computed with the centroids ∈C∗\in C^*∈C∗﻿, thus resulting in a much less computation time rather then with Ψ\PsiΨ﻿

We identify kkk﻿ distinct partitions (inverted list) L1,...,LkL_1, ..., L_kL1​,...,Lk​﻿ where Li={ψ∈Ψ:q(ψ)=μi∗}L_i = \{ \psi \in \Psi : q(\psi) = \mu_i^*\}Li​={ψ∈Ψ:q(ψ)=μi∗​}﻿

  • The set of LiL_iLi​﻿ is called Inverted File (IVF) that is saved in a vector DB, allowing to save them as tensor, to make computations in GPU
  • IVF index does not improve the space consumption, since it still needs to store
    all embeddings, but it can reduce the search time depending on the number of partitions

At query processing time, we specify to search for the NN document embeddings in p>0p > 0p>0﻿ partitions

  • If p=k,p = k,p=k,﻿ the search is exhaustive
  • If p<kp < kp<k﻿, the search is carried out in the partitions whose centroid is closer to the query embedding
    • I can sort the partitions wrt the distance of the query embeddings and the centroid of the partition LiL_iLi​﻿
    • Shouldn’t look just the closest one, because i could have a ψi\psi_iψi​﻿ closer to the query in another partitions → search is not exact
    • Curse of dimensionality → problem with all the comparison

In 2003, Google proposed a content-based image ranking algorithm to sort the matching images w.r.t. a image query based on the well known bag of words model for textual information

  • We save an image (collection or query) with a sequence of centroids indexes for each keypoint
  • Voronoi cells are called visual words
  • An image is quantised into visual words q1,...,qmq_1, ..., q_mq1​,...,qm​﻿. We compute TF-IDF:
    • where TF(qi,d)\text{TF}(q_i,d)TF(qi​,d)﻿ is the number of occurrences of the visual word qiq_iqi​﻿ within the image ddd﻿ (the local visual word weight)
    • IDF(qi)=log(nnqi)\text{IDF}(q_i) = log(\frac{n}{n_{qi}})IDF(qi​)=log(nqi​n​)﻿, where nnn﻿ is the number of indexed images and nqin_{qi}nqi​﻿
      is the number of indexed images in which the visual word qiq_iqi​﻿ appears (the global visual word weight)
